items.excerpt: Instrumental funk/soul bands are often spurned by the jazz aficionados as less serious than "real" jazz bands, but that would be a mistake with How Now Brown Cow. Despite the playfulness of the band name and song titles, in addition to having a great deal of fun playing, they are serious musicians and this is seriously good music.
items.body:
Instrumental funk/soul bands are often spurned by the jazz aficionados as less serious than "real" jazz bands, but that would be a mistake with How Now Brown Cow. Despite the playfulness of the band name and song titles, in addition to having a great deal of fun playing, they are serious musicians and this is seriously good music.

How Now Brown Cow has played in the Seattle, Washington community for more than a decade, often as a trio. This live recording from the Sea Monster Lodge, where the band plays regularly, showcases the improvisatory finesse of the band members, from Dave Kurtiak's thick, complicated bass runs to Donovan Pfeifer's solid groove on drums to Kerry O'Connor's funky keyboards. They are supplemented on this recording by Brad Schrandt on sax and flute, a frequent collaborator with the band. His contributions add a forceful texture to the songs and help elevate them even more.

The opener, "No Cat Having Bag," sets the tone for the album. A stomping funky number, the tune is pushed along by Kurtiak's pulsating, busy basslines and Pfeifer's stuttering stickwork, with Schrandt and O'Connor trading solos over the tight rhythm. The members complement each other and engage in keeping the sound fresh and exciting. Even when they slow it down in songs like "Pippity Poppity" and "South of No North," Kurtiak's fingers are moving up and down the bass neck to Pfeifer's steady beat, with O'Connor throwing accents from the keyboards. This is a band on the level of like-minded but better-known bands like Lettuce and Snarky Puppy.

The musical conversations they have on every song are engrossing as well as danceable, especially between O'Connor and Schrandt, working almost as call-and-response at times. The use of flute on a couple of songs offers a different, unexpected flavor. While a more muscular instrument like the sax is expected on funk songs rather than the more delicate flute, Schrandt uses the instrument on "Hang a Louie" to drive the song, while on "That Dog Don't Hunt" he lets the flute float above the cascading keyboard groove O'Connor lays down over a bouncing rhythm from Kurtiak and Pfeiffer.

Based on this recording, the band is definitely one to see live. Although the title is a bit misleading—there is nothing spoiled about this music. Drink it up and you will feel like the psychedelic cow of the cover, well-sated and a little woozy.

items.excerpt: A legend has grown up around the music Miles Davis created for Louis Malle's debut film Lift to the Scaffold (Ascenseur pour l'échafaud). The story goes that Davis arrived at the Paris studio having never seen the film. He watched the rushes once, then improvised as the footage rolled with his European quintet—Rene Urtreger on piano, Barney Wilen on tenor saxophone, Pierre Michelot on bass, and Kenny Clarke on drums. The music was recorded on the night of December 4 and 5, 1957.
items.body:
A legend has grown up around the music Miles Davis created for Louis Malle's debut film Lift to the Scaffold (Ascenseur pour l'échafaud). The story goes that Davis arrived at the Paris studio having never seen the film. He watched the rushes once, then improvised as the footage rolled with his European quintet—Rene Urtreger on piano, Barney Wilen on tenor saxophone, Pierre Michelot on bass, and Kenny Clarke on drums. The music was recorded on the night of December 4 and 5, 1957.

The circumstances surrounding the recording are central to its mythology, and the spontaneity was real: Davis was at the peak of his powers.

The film's plot concerns the hired murder of Jeanne Moreau's husband. The professional killer realizes, after the deed is done, that he has left crucial evidence at the scene. Returning to retrieve it, he becomes trapped in the building's lift.

1957 was a landmark year for Davis. In May he had recorded Miles Ahead (Columbia) with Gil Evans. In December came the groundbreaking Lift to the Scaffold sessions—and just four days before those recordings, Davis had played a concert at the Olympia in Paris with the same musicians.

He had come to Paris under contract to appear at the Club Saint-Germain, leaving his regular group behind in New York. By this point he was famous enough to draw crowds on his own. The ensemble he assembled was formidable. Barney Wilen was just twenty, fresh to the scene but already commanding. Pierre Michelot had played with Sidney Bechet and Clifford Brown. René Urtreger was the house pianist at the club and had accompanied Lester Young. Kenny Clarke—who had helped redefine jazz drumming in the 1940s—had made Paris his home. Beyond their residency at Saint-Germain, the group also played concerts in Brussels, Amsterdam, and Stuttgart.

Writer Boris Vian captured the atmosphere of the recording session: "This recording was made at night in the studios of the Paris broadcasting station, in a most informal atmosphere. Among those present was Jeanne Moreau, the principal star of the film. She proved a very charming hostess, serving refreshments to musicians and technicians at an improvised bar. There were those responsible for the production and the technical staff, but also Louis Mall—with his braces dangling loosely—doing his utmost to encourage Miles in his musical accompaniment of the film. The orchestra members, very much at ease in this informal atmosphere, looked at images from the principal scenes and, being thus in the right mood, improvised various musical paraphrases as the reel was projected.

"In the melody 'Dîner au motel' you will notice a curious sonority in Miles' trumpet. The explanation is a strange one: while he was playing, a tiny piece of skin from his lip came loose and stuck in the mouthpiece of his instrument. Miles gladly accepted this strange new element—in the most literal sense, an unheard-of musical effect—in quite the same way as those painters who owe the quality of a particular brushstroke to mere chance."

Little preparation had been done. Davis had sketched only a few simple harmonic sequences in his hotel room and shared them with the band shortly before recording began. With the plot explained, loops of key scenes were projected in the studio while the musicians improvised directly to the images, without any pre-composed themes. Bassist Pierre Michelot later recalled: "Miles just asked us to play two chords—D minor and C7, four bars of each, ad lib." It was typical of Davis: minimal instruction paired with an unerring sense of atmosphere.

By 1957, Davis had grown weary of the dense convolutions of bebop. This challenge gave him permission to slow down—and slow down he does, the music emphasising the film's Hitchcockian tension, its fatal romanticism and nocturnal menace.

Chronologically, the soundtrack sits only months before Kind of Blue (Columbia, 1959), and in many ways it points directly toward that masterpiece. For the first time, Davis fully committed to a modal approach—accepting harmonic limitations not as a constraint but as a means of focusing on pure line, emotion, and tone. As critic Ashley Kahn has noted, "Miles liked the results, and it forever changed how he would approach music and music-making. Eventually, it also changed the jazz world."

Davis's Harmon-muted trumpet is edgy, intimate, and almost corrosive throughout. "Générique" opens the film in an evocative, unhurried mood, giving Davis space to trace the loneliness of Moreau as she wanders the streets. "L'assassinat de Carala" is dark, menacing, and brooding, coiling the film's suspense tighter. "Sur l'autoroute" and "Dîner au motel" drive hard, showcasing Kenny Clarke's crisp brushwork, Wilen's quicksilver tenor, and Michelot's fluent bass. "Florence sur les Champs-Élysées" returns to pacing and melancholic restraint.

The current reissue presents the recordings across three formats. A 180g vinyl LP reproduces the original album in a gatefold tip-on sleeve, with an English translation of Boris Vian's original liner notes. A three-10" vinyl edition expands the release to include the full original soundtrack alongside the complete session takes from December 1957, housed in a three-panel gatefold with Franck Bergerot's essay A Present from Miles Davis to Louis Malle. A limited-edition two-CD set brings together the original album and all surviving takes from the sessions of 4 and 5 December, accompanied by a 60-page hardcover book featuring notes by Ashley Kahn and Franck Bergerot.

items.album: Just Stay Live, featuring Garth Hudson, Recorded Live At The Falcon
items.excerpt: With the late Garth Hudson's photo on such prominent display in Debra Clark's graphic design for Just Stay Live, featuring Garth Hudson, Recorded Live at the Falcon, the participation of the brilliant multi-instrumentalist of The Band threatens to overshadow the other attributes of Just Stay Live, most conspicuous of which is the courageous choice of material.
items.body:
With the late Garth Hudson's photo on such prominent display in Debra Clark's graphic design for Just Stay Live, featuring Garth Hudson, Recorded Live at the Falcon, the participation of the brilliant multi-instrumentalist of The Band threatens to overshadow the other attributes of Just Stay Live, most conspicuous of which is the courageous choice of material.

Lesser artists might be daunted by the prospect of covering songs by Gregg Allman ("It's Not My Cross To Bear"), Bob Dylan ("Knockin' On Heaven's Door"), and George Harrison ("Isn't It A Pity"). But also incorporating into the 11 selections comparably challenging numbers like Blind Willie Johnson's "John The Revelator" (made famous by Son House) and "Turn On Your Lovelight," the Alexis P. Suter Band acquits equally stylishly.

In fact, the latter R&B chestnut, interpreted by artists ranging from the Grateful Dead to the aforementioned younger sibling of the Allman Brothers Band, is indicative of the overall gusto of the performances by the quintet, which so often frequents the Woodstock environs of New York State (specifically with numerous appearances at the late Levon Helm's Midnight Ramble series of concerts).

Hudson's five minutes and two seconds of solo piano is hardly an exception. Much like his spotlights on stage with his now-deceased comrades—once known as The Hawks—he is unobtrusive as he elicits sounds from the ivories that range from the rhapsodic to the ruminative, then weaves them in and out of other arrangements.

In that sense, that cut is a microcosm of this program. Recorded (in Dolby Atmos Surround Sound) by Alan Douches at the Falcon Arts Center in Marlboro, New York, the sound is most robust as mixed and mastered by that same engineer. In fact, the subtlety of the audio fosters the resonance of the sonorous tones Suter shares with her co-singers Vicki Bell and Linda Pino on "Whistling in the Dark."

And yet, on this co-write of the former with Suter Band guitarist Jimmy Bennett, Peter Bennett's bass booms as much as Ray Grappone's drums rumble. Such sonic depth matches the well of emotions this ensemble draws upon during this roughly 70-plus minutes performance.

The uplifting likes of "Rise" may be the most exalting moments here, but not by much. The devotional overtones are unmistakable as they pervade this rendition of the aforementioned Beatle's number. Accordingly, that cut makes for a logical conclusion to this set because it simultaneously sounds like a benediction from the performers to their audience and a testimonial to the power of great soul music as on display throughout Just Stay Live.

items.excerpt: As guitarist in a trio setting, Jim Robitaille has to wear a number of hats: melodic, harmonic and improvisational. And on Sonic, the Massachusetts-based guitarist's ninth recording under his name, Robitaille dons one more headdress, as eight of the album's ten numbers are his original compositions.
items.body:
As guitarist in a trio setting, Jim Robitaille has to wear a number of hats: melodic, harmonic and improvisational. And on Sonic, the Massachusetts-based guitarist's ninth recording under his name, Robitaille dons one more headdress, as eight of the album's ten numbers are his original compositions.

Robitaille plays his parts well, as do his astute teammates: bassist Tom Casale and drummer Chris Poudrier. Even so, there is a persistent sameness throughout the session that seems to say, "Yes, this is good—but it's not getting any better."

That may be selling it short, as everyone is clearly giving the music his best shot, and there are decent solos along the way by Robitaille and Casale (and by Poudrier on the brisk "Room 554" and Miles Davis' "All Blues"). Robitaille's themes, on the other hand, are well-meaning but several rungs removed from impressive. The same tepidness holds true for "All Blues" and John Coltrane's gentle "Central Park West," neither of which showers sparks in the hands of a trio.

The opening number, "Stratus," moves into an affirmative gear after Robitaille's subtle guitar synth intro, and Casale takes the first solo before the leader adds a few incisive remarks. "Anthem," written for the late bassist and Robitaille colleague Bill Miele, enfolds a softer tone, as do "The Sea and the Sky," "Sonic" and "Blue Moon," which follow. "Pulse" imparts some rhythmic heat before "Central Park West" again lowers the temperature.

"Room 554" is the spiciest item on the menu, and everyone digs in hard to underline its rhythmic imprint, but placidity returns on the ethereal "Sound Origins," and "All Blues," even though hearty and well-played, seems rather out of place in a trio format.

Bottom line: a good but less than persuasive session whose appeal may be limited to those who appreciate the synergy of a trio, especially one whose focal point is a guitar.

items.excerpt: Dave Douglas has spent a career dodging his own shadow, and that restlessness is precisely what keeps his catalog from ever feeling stagnant. Transcend locates its friction point between two titans who seem unlikely to share the same oxygen: the spiritual grandeur of Duke Ellington's Sacred Concerts and the dense, mosaic canvases of painter Jack Whitten.
items.body:
Dave Douglas has spent a career dodging his own shadow, and that restlessness is precisely what keeps his catalog from ever feeling stagnant. Transcend locates its friction point between two titans who seem unlikely to share the same oxygen: the spiritual grandeur of Duke Ellington's Sacred Concerts and the dense, mosaic canvases of painter Jack Whitten.

The weight of the album rests on the chemistry of this specific quintet. With James Brandon Lewis on tenor, Tomeka Reid on cello, Rafiq Bhatia on guitar, and Ian Chang on drums, the music moves away from a traditional leader-and-sidemen setup toward something genuinely collective. Reid is a fresh voice in Douglas's orbit, and she fundamentally shifts the group's architecture. Cello can often feel like a novelty in jazz, but Reid integrates it so seamlessly into the harmonic floor that you quickly forget the instrument and simply hear the depth it adds.

The set opens with Ellington's "Come Sunday," played with a grit that favors atmosphere over reverence. Douglas avoids the trap of making the melody too precious. Instead, Bhatia's distortion-laced guitar rolls in like a storm front while Lewis enters with that signature, forceful tenor sound, pushing just enough against the melody to keep it from settling. The originals carry even more weight, particularly "Energy Fields," which feels unsettled in the best way as Chang drives a nervous pulse from underneath while Reid and Bhatia tangle in tactile textures, the whole thing morphing into Douglas' intense proclamations.

On "Gentle Collapse," Whitten's influence is most tangible—melodic fragments appear, dissolve, and reassemble in altered forms, mimicking the layered surfaces and broken symmetry of Whitten's canvases. "Heaven" serves as the emotional hinge, featuring Douglas and Lewis circling one another in near unisons that never quite lock. That microscopic gap between their notes is where the real drama lives, generating a sustained tension that only partially resolves.

Not everything lands with equal force. "Argle-Bargle" aims for a specific kind of jagged friction, but the moving parts never quite click into place. It feels more like eavesdropping on an interesting process than arriving at a satisfying payoff. Ellington's "Oclupaca," however, provides a welcome rhythmic snap to a set that often prefers texture over momentum.

Douglas skips the big theatrical finish and simply lets the sound evaporate into the room—a move that feels less like a conclusion and more like a mark of genuine confidence, trusting the listener to find their own way out.

items.excerpt: Two quotes come to mind in the wake of Simon Hanes' Gargantua. The first is from Perry Farrell of Jane's Addiction: "Camera got them images / Camera got them all / Nothing's shocking... " The second, often attributed to William S. Burroughs: "Nothing is true, everything is permitted." Taken together, they suggest a world where boundaries dissolve and meaning becomes fluid. Hanes both affirms and challenges that premise in this sprawling, provocative work.
items.body:
Two quotes come to mind in the wake of Simon Hanes' Gargantua. The first is from Perry Farrell of Jane's Addiction: "Camera got them images / Camera got them all / Nothing's shocking... " The second, often attributed to William S. Burroughs: "Nothing is true, everything is permitted." Taken together, they suggest a world where boundaries dissolve and meaning becomes fluid. Hanes both affirms and challenges that premise in this sprawling, provocative work.

Gargantua is written for an unconventional large ensemble: three drum kits, three electric basses, three trombones, three French horns, and three voices. The sheer scale of the instrumentation hints at excess, but the result is far from chaotic. Hanes, an acolyte of downtown icon John Zorn, has built a reputation for stylistic range, composing for his Italian soundtrack—inspired ensemble Tredici Bacci, the experimental surf project Tsons of Tsunami, the thrash/improv outfit Trigger, and a variety of contemporary classical contexts. Here, he brings those disparate threads into a single, ambitious statement.

The music operates like an intricate collage; layered, deliberate and densely referential. Hanes draws inspiration from a journey through Norway, the volcanic force of Iceland and Hawaii, and François Rabelais's 16th-century epic Gargantua and Pantagruel, a once-scandalous satire of giants and excess. To this he adds fragments of Buddhist texts, passages from Dante's Inferno, baroque gestures, minimalist repetition and the raw energy of rock and metal. On paper, the combination seems unwieldy; in practice, it recalls the eclectic logic of Frank Zappa's ensembles or Zorn's Naked City band, where unlikely elements cohere through force of vision.

Across the album's ten tracks, there are no featured soloists. The emphasis is squarely on composition and collective execution. The fifteen musicians function as a single, shifting organism, navigating Hanes' abrupt transitions and layered structures. The journey is global and temporal: ancient philosophies collide with modern noise, sacred texts meet irreverent outbursts. "Submit to the Fabulosity," for instance, blends disco-inflected rhythms with percussive density, while its vocalists deliver a barrage of profane invective. Elsewhere, "Moirai" offers a moment of fragile, almost sacred vocal harmony, only to be shattered by the abrasive intensity of "Lacerated by a Flying Shard."

Hanes moves freely between extremes, baroque intricacy and heavy-metal force, serene minimalism and explosive noise, linking Stravinsky to Led Zeppelin, alpine folk traditions to contemporary experimentalism. The result is music that feels both overwhelming and meticulously constructed, a constant oscillation between order and rupture.

Gargantua is not an easy listen, nor is it meant to be. It is a demanding, immersive work that unfolds more fully with repeated exposure. What initially registers as excess reveals itself, over time, as a carefully shaped landscape of contrasts. In the end, Hanes doesn't simply argue that "nothing is shocking," he suggests that meaning still emerges from the collision of ideas, that even in a world without clear boundaries, form and purpose can be forged.

items.body:
Live at Blue LLama by the David Janeway Trio was recorded in June 2024 at the Blue LLama Jazz Club in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and it is the kind of album that is unforced, deeply conversational, and grounded in a shared musical trust. Pianist Janeway has long valued rhythmic authority and melodic clarity over display and possesses a composer's sense of proportion. He is paired with Billy Hart, a drummer whose influence spans generations, and Robert Hurst, a bassist deeply rooted in the Detroit tradition he shares with Janeway, whose playing is at once foundational and lyrical.

The set opens with Jerome Kern's "All the Things You Are." Janeway begins with a reflective solo-piano introduction, then moves into motion with an Afro-Cuban montuno figure. It is not a stylistic pivot but a rebalancing of the tune's structure. Hart's cymbal work and Hurst's anchored pulse give Janeway room to stretch the rhythm without losing the thread. Thad Jones's "A Child is Born" is a study in restraint. Janeway's phrasing is patient, allowing each note to settle. Hurst and Hart provide an unobtrusive foundation, turning the waltz into something that feels suspended rather than counted.

"Forward Motion" is one of Janeway's originals, showcasing his compositional clarity. The themes are clearly stated, then expanded and reshaped during the performance. The supporting rhythmic cushion pays tribute to Herbie Hancock's "Maiden Voyage." The popular standard "Sweet and Lovely" finds Hurst stepping forward with a presence that is both melodic and structural. His lines not only provide support but also serve as a launching pad for the trio to respond collectively in real time.

The trio's shared history is rooted in the aforementioned Detroit tradition and carries a dual weight. First, an unshakeable commitment to groove, and second, a deep-rooted sense of community. The feeling of time is not only lived in but also binds the music together. Just as important is the ethic behind it, the spirit of giving back, of sharing knowledge and experience, and of collective uplift.

Gary Peacock's "Gardenia" becomes one of the session's most introspective moments. Janeway and Hurst dwell together in space and tone, while Hart's sensitive, warm locomotion allows the emotional weight to build gradually. Continuing this search for self-awareness, the Billy Strayhorn composition "Star-Crossed Lovers" provides the perfect vehicle. Janeway handles the theme with care, preserving its harmonic tensions rather than smoothing them over.

The closing sequence is where the trio's full breadth comes into focus. McCoy Tyner's "Search for Peace" is rendered by Janeway with spiritual intensity that builds organically and without pause. It gives way to "Blues on the Corner," and the transition feels inevitable, not contrived. Janeway, Hurst, and Hart exchange musical ideas, shifting from inward searching to rhythmic declaration.

What lingers is not any particular moment but a sense of patience in the players' interactions and a willingness to let the ideas develop, which speaks to a process of building a shared language and a mutual perspective.

items.body:
Callum Au is not one for half measures. As an arranger he has worked with international orchestras and contributed to movie scores; as a performer he is an in-demand session trombonist. He steps into the spotlight with Sing Seven Seas, a project of genuinely epic ambition: 81 musicians, a voiceover artist, 16 compositions and nearly two hours of music. The album explores classic swing, progressive orchestral arrangements and contemporary jazz, with Au contributing trombone alongside a remarkable cast of cross-generational talent.

While conceived as a single project, the music falls into two volumes, the first highlights Au's compositions across a variety of styles, the second draws on the big band tradition and pays tribute to his influences.

Opening track: "Swipe Right!" is intended to capture the age of Instagram and TikTok but conjures up the atmosphere of the 1920s rather than the 2020s. Nonetheless, Au's arrangement is fluid and tight, the trombone cascade delights and Duncan Hemstock adds a terrific clarinet solo—leaving you with a broad smile regardless of the decade.

Jake Wilson's electric guitar and Nadim Teimoori's tenor saxophone are the clear highlights cutting through the dense structure of "Galt's Motor." "Si Vis Pacem Para Carnyx," a nod to the Iron Age Celtic wind instrument, opens in cinematic orchestral fashion before the focus shifts to a traditional folk band, but the two worlds never convincingly merge or complement each other, with the track stretching on longer than the idea can sustain.

Au's skills as an arranger and trombonist shine on "Murmurations," making it one of the album's highlights. Equally enjoyable is "The Weaver," where the lilting melody gives Teimoori another opportunity to impress. "Jazz AI" is a terrific romp in which artificial intelligence runs amok at a conservatoire. Kate Emmerton's words, narrated by Matt Forbes, set the scene for Au's trombone, Emma Rawicz's tenor saxophone and James Davison's flugelhorn to contribute brilliantly to the mayhem.

Au seems more at home on the second volume, drawing on the influences of Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Kenny Wheeler and others who have shaped his musical voice. The big band blast of "Bandwagon Blues" swings with swagger, driven by solo exchanges and shifting ensemble combinations. Jointly composed by Au and his son, "Through The Deep Dark Woods" is inventive and playful, while the Latin rhythms of "Caledonian Sun God" bring out excellent contributions from pianist Rob Barron and trumpeter Ryan Quigley.

The ensemble are on top of their game all through the recording, as are all the principal soloists, with Freddie Gavita's flugelhorn and Martin Williams' tenor saxophone showcased on "Fork Hen" and Simon Marsh's alto saxophone a feature on "Verity."

items.excerpt: A miniature doll-like effigy of the great country music singer-songwriter Dolly Parton adorns the cover of trumpeter-composer Matt White's Dolly. How did the Queen of Country become the subject of this fascinating (if awkwardly-branded) mainstream jazz album? Happenstance.
items.body:
A miniature doll-like effigy of the great country music singer-songwriter Dolly Parton adorns the cover of trumpeter-composer Matt White's Dolly. How did the Queen of Country become the subject of this fascinating (if awkwardly-branded) mainstream jazz album? Happenstance.

White was researching Gullah songs for his 2023 album, Lowcountry (Ropeadope), when YouTube "Pandorized" him into a video of a young Parton, guitar in hand, performing "The Bridge," solo, on the Porter Wagoner television show in the '60s. He made a rhythmic connection, and—voilà—the seed was planted.

Working with Liz Kelley, the project's excellent vocalist, White created a little dogma for himself, a set of arranging rules: Keep the vocal melodies and lyrics the same, keep the original keys and all the modulations. "Everything else was open to change." Kelley serves as a solid stand-in for Parton. Her singing style is country—with the requisite cry and twang—but she manages to avoid imitation, coming across as genuine. White has her holding down the melodic fort sans improvisation, which (ties her up you might say, but) frees the band to respond to Parton's songs in a jazz milieu without altering their most recognizeable feature, the vocal line.

The settings are engaging and complex, full of jazz harmonies, melodies and rhythms. And the instrumentalists are superb players and improvisers. Their lines swirl around the vocal ones, alternately in call-and-response fashion, contrapuntally, via ostinatos, in fills and instrumental breaks, and through solo statements.

Between heartwrenching songs of "bad men and birds" (as Kelley put it) written by a very young Parton, "9 to 5" appears in three riveting instrumental settings that feature the powerful rhythm team of Demetrius Doctor on organ and Colleen Clark on drums, preaching the gospel of a hard day's work in brief two-to-three-minute sermons (with fairly equal parts gravity, levity, and liberty). You might even sense a bit of Bud Powell's "Parisian Thoroughfare" (Clifford Brown & Max Roach, Capitol, 1954).

As invigorating and beautifully-performed as the vocal arrangments are, the three instrumental versions of "9 to 5," interspersed throughout the program, stop the show with their freedom and abstraction.

Throughout, the sound of the band is striking. On top are Kelley's vocal eloquence and the fleet grace of White's cornet (he bought one for the occasion), along with Tim Fischer's lyrical guitar. On the bottom, Doctor's prodigious organ and Clark's sizzling, crackling drums, which sometimes walk the line between jazz and country idioms. This is an unusual album without a doubt, one worth more than just a few spins.

items.body:
As if producer and archival sleuth Zev Feldman weren't already busy enough unearthing lost jazz treasures, he has recently launched a new imprint, Time Traveler. A devoted collector in his own right, Feldman has turned his attention—at least initially—to the storied catalog of Muse Records. Founded in 1972 by Joe Fields, with significant contributions from Don Schlitten, Muse weathered the shifting tides of the industry for a quarter century. While portions of the catalog have resurfaced on CD over the years, Time Traveler now delivers these titles back to their intended analog format, marking their first vinyl reissues since the original pressings.

Following earlier Muse revivals featuring Roy Brooks, Carlos Garnett, Kenny Barron, Larry Young/Joe Chambers, and Woody Shaw, Buster Williams' Pinnacle receives the Record Store Day treatment. This 1975 session is presented with care: mastering by Matt Lutthans, pressing at Optimal Media, a Stoughton tip-on jacket, and newly commissioned liner notes accompanied by a period photograph of Williams.

Recorded in the wake of Williams' tenure with Herbie Hancock's groundbreaking Mwandishi ensemble, Pinnacle carries forward many of that group's exploratory, groove-oriented sensibilities. The expansive opener, "The Hump," unfolds with a serpentine pulse, its bass clarinet textures and collective improvisation later finding new life through sampling by The Fugees and A Tribe Called Quest. Williams' bass navigates the shifting Latin undercurrents of "Noble Ego," enriched by wordless vocals and the percussive colors of Guilherme Franco. The title track closes side one with a striking, angular theme voiced by trumpet, saxophones, and ensemble vocals, with both Shaw and Sonny Fortune contributing concise but memorable solos.

Side two opens with the fluid, gliding lines of "Tayamisha," where Williams' melodic sensibility gives way to a firmly swinging feel. Fortune's soprano cuts through with angular phrasing, while Onaje Allan Gumbs adds depth on acoustic piano, supported throughout by the responsive drumming of Billy Hart. Any notion that straight-ahead swing had fallen out of favor in the 1970s is quickly dispelled. The shimmering Rhodes textures of "Batuki" bring the session to a close, its laid-back funk underscored by Fortune's luminous flute work and an especially commanding presence from Shaw's trumpet.

Ultimately, Pinnacle stands as a vivid reminder of a fertile, often underappreciated period in jazz. With this thoughtfully produced reissue, Feldman once again makes a compelling case for revisiting the margins of the canon—where, more often than not, the real discoveries await.

items.excerpt: Guitarist Bobby Broom is no stranger to the music of tenor saxophonist Sonny Rollins, having spent two tours of duty with various Rollins groups which, taken together, add up to a decade (1982-'87 and 2005-'10). Notes of Thanks is Broom's way of expressing his gratitude to Rollins for those years in the trenches and the many valuable lessons he learned there, the best way he knows how: through his music.
items.body:
Guitarist Bobby Broom is no stranger to the music of tenor saxophonist Sonny Rollins, having spent two tours of duty with various Rollins groups which, taken together, add up to a decade (1982-'87 and 2005-'10). Notes of Thanks is Broom's way of expressing his gratitude to Rollins for those years in the trenches and the many valuable lessons he learned there, the best way he knows how: through his music.

Rollins wrote every song on Notes of Thanks save one, bassist Dennis Carroll's easygoing "Me Time." The third member of Broom's Chicago-based trio is drummer Kobie Watkins. Even though Broom is among the best at what he does, and his teammates are likewise sharp and skillful, there is only so much a trio can do to engender variety, no matter how perceptive and charming the music.

With that in mind, it should be noted that there are not many guitar-led trios as proficient as this one, and that Rollins' tunes are for the most part astute and engaging, starting with the good-natured "Alfie's Theme" (not to be confused with the "Alfie" written by Burt Bacharach and Hal David for the 1966 film of that name), on which Broom delivers the first of his sharp and measured solos, enhanced by a brief nod to Joshua and the battle of Jericho.

"The Freedom Suite, Part 1" is next, followed by one of Rollins' more well-known tunes, the amiable and rhythmic "Doxy." Carroll takes one of his admirable solos there, while Watkins displays his deftness at the drum kit. It is not until later—the last two numbers, in fact—that Broom and his mates delve into any other Rollins classics, namely the high-stepping "Pent Up House" and canorous "Valse Hot." They are preceded by the lesser-known "Allison," "Kim," "Paul's Pal" and "Strode Road."

A largely agreeable studio session for trio (and Rollins) fans with an extra half-star for exemplary teamwork and musicianship.

items.body:
Jazz artist, producer, and composer Darryl Alexander Sr. began developing his skills as a musician in his school band playing trombone, tuba, and drums. Alexander began his recording career with his debut release titled Coast to Coast (1992) followed by 17th Street (1995), both on the Prestige jazz label.

"Writing Our Story" opens with a slow, reflective tenor saxophone melody from Jeff Kashiwa. As Ken Karsh enters on rhythm guitar, the composition begins to unfold with a sense of quiet intensity. Momentum builds with the soulful single "Seen It Before." Jackiem Joyner's soprano saxophone introduces an upbeat groove, supported by Wilbur Krebs on electric bass. Keyboard and guitar solos from Alexander and Karsh add depth and movement. "Rise Up" brings a smooth, funky rhythm, with Kenny Blake's alto saxophone delivering a sweet and engaging melody. Pete Tokar's piano solo blends seamlessly into the track's flow.

A shift in texture arrives with "Sunset After 7" where Latin-inspired percussion and tropical horn elements create a warm, atmospheric feel. Soft piano by Alton Merrell. The track closes with a tasteful acoustic guitar solo by Karsh. "Didn't See It Coming" stands out as a highlight. Kashiwa and Tokar create a strong musical dialogue, supported by a rich rhythm section. The slow groove allows space for expressive phrasing, culminating in a beautifully controlled ending. "Wonders of Your Love" offers a mid-tempo ballad featuring Jeff Green on soprano saxophone, complemented by Karsh's subtle guitar work.

"Intrigued" continues the smooth jazz aesthetic, with Kashiwa delivering a soulful tenor saxophone performance that is both relaxed and expressive. "High Road" unfolds gradually, with Tokar's piano and Rhodes guiding a winding melodic path that fades gently. "Almost There" introduces layered textures, combining Kenny Blake's alto saxophone with Alexander's keyboard work and rhythmic programming. Guitar solo by Karsh and solo by Croes on Rhodes add dimension. "Pacific Blue" maintains the album's momentum, with Blake's alto saxophone leading into a groove supported by guitar and Rhodes. The energy peaks with "No Middle Ground," where percussion, bass, and saxophone drive an upbeat and confident arrangement. Karsh's electric guitar solo adds a strong finishing touch.

Morning Calls moves with intention, blending smooth jazz textures with layered instrumentation and collaborative energy. Each track contributes to a narrative shaped by melody, groove, and refined musicianship.
